Main.sentence: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration ( NASA /ˈnæsə/ ) is an ___E:independent agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_agencies_of_the_United_States_government)___ of the ___E:US federal government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States)___ responsible for the United States's civil ___E:space program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_government_space_agencies)___ and for research in ___E:aeronautics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics)___ and ___E:space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space)___ exploration.

Headquartered in ___E:Washington, D.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.)___ , NASA operates ten field centers across the United States and is organized into mission directorates for Science, Space Operations, Exploration Systems Development, Space Technology, ___E:Aeronautics Research U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics_Research_Mission_Directorate)___ , and Mission Support. ___E:Established in 1958 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Act)___ , NASA succeeded the ___E:National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Advisory_Committee_for_Aeronautics)___ (NACA) to give the American space development effort a distinct civilian orientation, emphasizing peaceful applications in ___E:space science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_science)___ .

It has since led most of America's ___E:space exploration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_exploration)___ programs, including ___E:Project Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury)___ , ___E:Project Gemini U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini)___ , the 1968–1972 ___E:Apollo program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program)___ missions, the ___E:Skylab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylab)___ space station, and the ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ .
The agency maintains major ground and communications infrastructure including the ___E:Deep Space Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Deep_Space_Network)___ and the Near Space Network.

NASA's science division is focused on better understanding Earth through the ___E:Earth Observing System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_Observing_System)___ ; advancing ___E:heliophysics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliophysics)___ through the efforts of the ___E:Science Mission Directorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Mission_Directorate)___ 's Heliophysics Research Program; exploring bodies throughout the ___E:Solar System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System)___ with advanced ___E:robotic spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotic_spacecraft)___ such as New Horizons and ___E:planetary rovers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rover_(space_exploration))___ such as Perseverance ; and researching ___E:astrophysics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrophysics)___ topics, such as the ___E:Big Bang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang)___ , through the ___E:James Webb Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)___ , the four ___E:Great Observatories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Observatories_program)___ (including the ___E:Hubble Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope)___ ), and associated programs.

The ___E:Launch Services Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_Services_Program)___ oversees launch operations for its ___E:uncrewed launches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncrewed_NASA_missions)___ .

NASA supports the ___E:International Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station)___ (ISS) along with the ___E:Commercial Crew Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Program)___ and oversees the development of the ___E:Orion spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(spacecraft))___ and the ___E:Space Launch System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_System)___ for the lunar ___E:Artemis program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program)___ .

It maintains programmatic partnerships with agencies such as ___E:ESA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ , ___E:JAXA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA)___ , ___E:CSA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency)___ , ___E:Roscosmos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos)___ (for ISS operations), ___E:NOAA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration)___ , and the ___E:USGS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey)___ .

NASA’s missions and media operations—such as ___E:NASA TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_TV)___ , ___E:Astronomy Picture of the Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy_Picture_of_the_Day)___ , and the ___E:NASA+ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA%2B)___ streaming service—have maintained high public visibility and contributed to spaceflight outreach in the United States and abroad.

A subject of ___E:numerous major films U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Films_about_NASA)___ , NASA has maintained an influence on American popular culture since the ___E:Apollo 11 mission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11_in_popular_culture)___ in 1969. For FY2022, Congress authorized a $24.041 billion budget, with a civil-service workforce of roughly 18,400; as of 2025, the acting administrator is ___E:Sean Duffy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Duffy)___ .
NASA traces its roots to the ___E:National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Advisory_Committee_for_Aeronautics)___ (NACA).

Despite ___E:Dayton, Ohio being the birthplace of aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayton,_Ohio#Birthplace_of_aviation)___ , by 1914 the United States recognized that it was far behind Europe in aviation capability.

Determined to regain American leadership in aviation, the ___E:United States Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ created the ___E:Aviation Section U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_Section,_U.S._Signal_Corps)___ of the US Army Signal Corps in 1914 and established NACA in 1915 to foster aeronautical research and development.

Over the next forty years, NACA would conduct aeronautical research in support of the ___E:US Air Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force)___ , ___E:US Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Army)___ , ___E:US Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Navy)___ , and the civil aviation sector.

After the end of ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , NACA became interested in the possibilities of guided missiles and supersonic aircraft, developing and testing the ___E:Bell X-1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_X-1)___ in a joint program with the ___E:US Air Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force)___ .
NACA's interest in space grew out of its rocketry program at the Pilotless Aircraft Research Division.

The Soviet Union's launch of ___E:Sputnik 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1)___ ushered in the ___E:Space Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Age)___ and kicked off the ___E:Space Race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race)___ .

Despite NACA's early rocketry program, the responsibility for launching the first American satellite fell to the ___E:Naval Research Laboratory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Research_Laboratory)___ 's ___E:Project Vanguard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Vanguard)___ , whose operational issues ensured the ___E:Army Ballistic Missile Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Ballistic_Missile_Agency)___ would launch ___E:Explorer 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer_1)___ , America's first satellite, on February 1, 1958.

The ___E:Eisenhower Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenhower_Administration)___ decided to split the United States's military and civil spaceflight programs, which were organized together under the ___E:Department of Defense's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ ___E:Advanced Research Projects Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Research_Projects_Agency)___ .

NASA was established on July 29, 1958, with the signing of the ___E:National Aeronautics and Space Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Act)___ and it began operations on October 1, 1958.
As the American's premier aeronautics agency, NACA formed the core of NASA's new structure by reassigning 8,000 employees and three major research laboratories.

NASA also proceeded to absorb the Naval Research Laboratory's Project Vanguard, the Army's ___E:Jet Propulsion Laboratory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory)___ (JPL), and the ___E:Army Ballistic Missile Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Ballistic_Missile_Agency)___ under ___E:Wernher von Braun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wernher_von_Braun)___ .
This left NASA firmly as the United States's civil space lead and the Air Force as the military space lead.
Plans for human spaceflight began in the US Armed Forces prior to NASA's creation.

The Air Force's ___E:Man in Space Soonest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_in_Space_Soonest)___ project formed in 1956,  coupled with the Army's Project Adam, served as the foundation for ___E:Project Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury)___ .

NASA established the ___E:Space Task Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Task_Group)___ to manage the program,  which would conduct crewed sub-orbital flights with the Army's ___E:Redstone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_Launch_Vehicle)___ rockets and orbital flights with the Air Force's ___E:Atlas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Atlas)___ launch vehicles.
While NASA intended for its first astronauts to be civilians, President Eisenhower directed that they be selected from the military.
The ___E:Mercury 7 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_7)___ astronauts included three Air Force pilots, three Navy aviators, and one Marine Corps pilot.

On May 5, 1961, ___E:Alan Shepard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shepard)___ became the first American to enter space, performing a suborbital spaceflight in the ___E:Freedom 7 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_3)___ .
This flight occurred less than a month after the Soviet ___E:Yuri Gagarin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin)___ became the first human in space, executing a full orbital spaceflight.

NASA's first orbital spaceflight was conducted by ___E:John Glenn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn)___ on February 20, 1962, in the ___E:Friendship 7 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_6)___ , making three full orbits before reentering.
Glenn had to fly parts of his final two orbits manually due to an autopilot malfunction.

The sixth and final Mercury mission was flown by ___E:Gordon Cooper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Cooper)___ in May 1963, performing 22 orbits over 34 hours in the ___E:Faith 7 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Atlas_9)___ .

The Mercury Program was wildly recognized as a resounding success, achieving its objectives to orbit a human in space, develop tracking and control systems, and identify other issues associated with human spaceflight.
While much of NASA's attention turned to space, it did not put aside its aeronautics mission.

Early aeronautics research attempted to build upon the X-1's ___E:supersonic flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersonic_flight)___ to build an aircraft capable of ___E:hypersonic flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_flight)___ .

The ___E:North American X-15 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_X-15)___ was a joint NASA–US Air Force program,  with the hypersonic test aircraft becoming the first non-dedicated spacecraft to cross from the atmosphere to outer space.

The X-15 also served as a testbed for Apollo program technologies, as well as ___E:ramjet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramjet)___ and ___E:scramjet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scramjet)___ propulsion.

Escalations in the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ between the United States and Soviet Union prompted President ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ to charge NASA with landing an American on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth by the end of the 1960s and installed ___E:James E. Webb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_E._Webb)___ as NASA administrator to achieve this goal.  On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy openly declared this goal in his "Urgent National Needs" speech to the United States Congress, declaring:
I believe this Nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth.
No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.

Kennedy gave his " ___E:We choose to go to the Moon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_choose_to_go_to_the_Moon)___ " speech the next year, on September 12, 1962 at ___E:Rice University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_University)___ , where he addressed the nation hoping to reinforce public support for the Apollo program.

Despite attacks on the goal of landing astronauts on the Moon from the former president Dwight Eisenhower and 1964 presidential candidate ___E:Barry Goldwater U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Goldwater)___ , President Kennedy was able to protect NASA's growing budget, of which 50% went directly to human spaceflight and it was later estimated that, at its height, 5% of Americans worked on some aspect of the Apollo program.

Mirroring the Department of Defense's program management concept using redundant systems in building the first intercontinental ballistic missiles, NASA requested the Air Force assign Major General ___E:Samuel C. Phillips U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_C._Phillips)___ to the space agency where he would serve as the director of the Apollo program.

Development of the ___E:Saturn V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V)___ rocket was led by Wernher von Braun and his team at the ___E:Marshall Space Flight Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Space_Flight_Center)___ , derived from the Army Ballistic Missile Agency's original ___E:Saturn I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_I)___ .

The ___E:Apollo spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_command_and_service_module)___ was designed and built by ___E:North American Aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Aviation)___ , while the ___E:Apollo Lunar Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Lunar_Module)___ was designed and built by ___E:Grumman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grumman)___ .
To develop the spaceflight skills and equipment required for a lunar mission, NASA initiated ___E:Project Gemini U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini)___ .
Using a modified Air Force ___E:Titan II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_II_GLV)___ launch vehicle, the Gemini capsule could hold two astronauts for flights of over two weeks.

Gemini pioneered the use of ___E:fuel cells U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cells)___ instead of batteries, and conducted the first American ___E:spacewalks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalks)___ and ___E:rendezvous operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rendezvous)___ .
The ___E:Ranger Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranger_Program)___ was started in the 1950s as a response to Soviet lunar exploration, however most missions ended in failure.

The ___E:Lunar Orbiter program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Orbiter_program)___ had greater success, mapping the surface in preparation for Apollo landings, conducting meteoroid detection, and measuring radiation levels.
The ___E:Surveyor program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_program)___ conducted uncrewed lunar landings and takeoffs, as well as taking surface and regolith observations.
Despite the setback caused by the ___E:Apollo 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_1)___ fire, which killed three astronauts, the program proceeded.

___E:Apollo 8 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_8)___ was the first crewed ___E:spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft)___ to leave ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ and the first ___E:human spaceflight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight)___ to reach the ___E:Moon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon)___ .
The crew orbited the Moon ten times on December 24 and 25, 1968, and then traveled safely back to ___E:Earth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth)___ .

The three Apollo 8 astronauts— ___E:Frank Borman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Borman)___ , ___E:James Lovell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Lovell)___ , and ___E:William Anders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Anders)___ —were the first humans to see the Earth as a globe in space, the first to witness an ___E:Earthrise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise)___ , and the first to see and manually photograph the far side of the Moon.

The first lunar landing was conducted by Apollo 11. Commanded by ___E:Neil Armstrong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong)___ with astronauts ___E:Buzz Aldrin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzz_Aldrin)___ and ___E:Michael Collins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Collins_(astronaut))___ , Apollo 11 was one of the most significant missions in NASA's history, marking the end of the ___E:Space Race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race)___ when the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ gave up its lunar ambitions.
As the first human to step on the surface of the Moon, Neil Armstrong uttered the now famous words:
That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
NASA would conduct six total lunar landings as part of the Apollo program, with ___E:Apollo 17 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17)___ concluding the program in 1972.
Wernher von Braun had advocated for NASA to develop a space station since the agency was created.

In 1973, following the end of the Apollo lunar missions, NASA launched its first space station, ___E:Skylab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylab)___ , on the final launch of the Saturn V. Skylab reused a significant amount of Apollo and Saturn hardware, with a repurposed Saturn V third stage serving as the primary module for the space station.
Damage to Skylab during its launch required spacewalks to be performed by the first crew to make it habitable and operational.

Skylab hosted nine missions and was decommissioned in 1974 and deorbited in 1979, two years prior to the first launch of the ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ and any possibility of boosting its orbit.

In 1975, the ___E:Apollo–Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo%E2%80%93Soyuz)___ mission was the first ever international spaceflight and a major diplomatic accomplishment between the Cold War rivals, which also marked the last flight of the Apollo capsule.
Flown in 1975, a US Apollo spacecraft docked with a Soviet ___E:Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft))___ capsule.
During the 1960s, NASA started its ___E:space science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_science)___ and interplanetary probe program.

The ___E:Mariner program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_program)___ was its flagship program, launching probes to ___E:Venus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus)___ , ___E:Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars)___ , and ___E:Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet))___ in the 1960s.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory was the lead NASA center for robotic interplanetary exploration, making significant discoveries about the ___E:inner planets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets)___ .

Despite these successes, Congress was unwilling to fund further interplanetary missions and NASA Administrator James Webb suspended all future interplanetary probes to focus resources on the Apollo program.
Following the conclusion of the Apollo program, NASA resumed launching interplanetary probes and expanded its ___E:space science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_science)___ program.
The first planet tagged for exploration was ___E:Venus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus)___ , sharing many similar characteristics to Earth.
First visited by American ___E:Mariner 2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_2)___ spacecraft,  Venus was observed to be a hot and inhospitable planet.

Follow-on missions included the ___E:Pioneer Venus project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Venus_project)___ in the 1970s and ___E:Magellan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_(spacecraft))___ , which performed radar mapping of Venus' surface in the 1980s and 1990s.
Future missions were flybys of Venus, on their way to other destinations in the Solar System.

___E:Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars)___ has long been a planet of intense fascination for NASA, being suspected of potentially having harbored life. ___E:Mariner 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_5)___ was the first NASA spacecraft to flyby Mars,  followed by ___E:Mariner 6 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_6)___ and ___E:Mariner 7 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_7)___ . ___E:Mariner 9 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_9)___ was the first orbital mission to Mars. Launched in 1975, ___E:Viking program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_program)___ consisted of two landings on Mars in 1976. Follow-on missions would not be launched until 1996, with the ___E:Mars Global Surveyor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Global_Surveyor)___ orbiter and ___E:Mars Pathfinder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Pathfinder)___ , deploying the first Mars rover, ___E:Sojourner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sojourner_(rover))___ .

During the early 2000s, the ___E:2001 Mars Odyssey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Mars_Odyssey)___ orbiter reached the planet and in 2004 the Sprit and Opportunity rovers landed on the Red Planet.
This was followed in 2005 by the ___E:Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Reconnaissance_Orbiter)___ and 2007 Phoenix Mars lander.

The 2012 landing of Curiosity discovered that the radiation levels on Mars were equal to those on the ___E:International Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station)___ , greatly increasing the possibility of Human exploration, and observed the key chemical ingredients for life to occur.

In 2013, the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution ( ___E:MAVEN U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAVEN)___ ) mission observed the Martian upper atmosphere and space environment and in 2018, the Interior exploration using Seismic Investigations Geodesy, and Heat Transport ( ___E:InSight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InSight)___ ) studied the Martian interior.
The 2021 Perseverance rover carried the first extraplanetary aircraft, a helicopter named Ingenuity .

NASA also launched missions to ___E:Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet))___ in 2004, with the MESSENGER probe demonstrating as the first use of a ___E:solar sail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_sail)___ .
NASA also launched probes to the ___E:outer Solar System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Solar_System)___ starting in the 1960s.
Pioneer 10 was the first probe to the outer planets, flying by ___E:Jupiter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter)___ , while Pioneer 11 provided the first close up view of the planet.
Both probes became the first objects to leave the Solar System.

The ___E:Voyager program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_program)___ launched in 1977, conducting flybys of ___E:Jupiter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter)___ and ___E:Saturn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn)___ , ___E:Neptune U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune)___ , and ___E:Uranus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus)___ on a trajectory to leave the Solar System.

The Galileo spacecraft, deployed from the Space Shuttle flight ___E:STS-34 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-34)___ , was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, discovering evidence of subsurface oceans on the ___E:Europa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon))___ and observed that the moon may hold ice or liquid water.

A joint NASA- ___E:European Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ - ___E:Italian Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Space_Agency)___ mission, ___E:Cassini–Huygens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassini%E2%80%93Huygens)___ , was sent to ___E:Saturn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn)___ 's moon ___E:Titan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(moon))___ , which, along with Mars and Europa, are the only celestial bodies in the Solar System suspected of being capable of harboring life.  Cassini discovered three new moons of Saturn and the ___E:Huygens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huygens_(spacecraft))___ probe entered Titan's atmosphere.

The mission discovered evidence of liquid hydrocarbon lakes on Titan and subsurface water oceans on the moon of ___E:Enceladus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus)___ , which could harbor life. Finally launched in 2006, the ___E:New Horizons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Horizons)___ mission was the first spacecraft to visit ___E:Pluto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto)___ and the ___E:Kuiper belt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuiper_belt)___ .
Beyond interplanetary probes, NASA has launched many ___E:space telescopes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_telescopes)___ .

Launched in the 1960s, the ___E:Orbiting Astronomical Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiting_Astronomical_Observatory)___ were NASA's first orbital telescopes,  providing ultraviolet, gamma-ray, x-ray, and infrared observations.

NASA launched the ___E:Orbiting Geophysical Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiting_Geophysical_Observatory)___ in the 1960s and 1970s to look down at Earth and observe its interactions with the Sun. The ___E:Uhuru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_(satellite))___ satellite was the first dedicated x-ray telescope, mapping 85% of the sky and discovering a large number of ___E:black holes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_holes)___ .
Launched in the 1990s and early 2000s, the ___E:Great Observatories program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Observatories_program)___ are among NASA's most powerful telescopes.

The ___E:Hubble Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope)___ was launched in 1990 on ___E:STS-31 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-31)___ from the Discovery and could view galaxies 15 billion light years away.  A major defect in the telescope's mirror could have crippled the program, had NASA not used computer enhancement to compensate for the imperfection and launched five Space Shuttle servicing flights to replace the damaged components.

The ___E:Compton Gamma Ray Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_Gamma_Ray_Observatory)___ was launched from the Atlantis on ___E:STS-37 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-37)___ in 1991, discovering a possible source of ___E:antimatter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter)___ at the center of the ___E:Milky Way U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milky_Way)___ and observing that the majority of gamma-ray bursts occur outside of the Milky Way galaxy.

The first tentative steps of returning to crewed lunar missions will be ___E:Artemis II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_II)___ , which is to include the Orion crew module, propelled by the SLS, and is expected to launch no later than April 2026. As of March 2022, NASA has awarded contracts for robotic lunar probes to companies such as ___E:Intuitive Machines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuitive_Machines)___ , ___E:Firefly Space Systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefly_Space_Systems)___ , and ___E:Astrobotic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrobotic)___ .

Artemis I launched on November 16, 2022, and returned to Earth safely on December 11, 2022. As of April 2025, NASA plans to launch Artemis II in April 2026.  and Artemis III in 2027.  Additional Artemis missions, ___E:Artemis IV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_IV)___ , ___E:Artemis V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_V)___ , and ___E:Artemis VI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_VI)___ are planned to launch between 2028 and 2031.

NASA's next major space initiative is the construction of the ___E:Lunar Gateway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Gateway)___ , a small space station in ___E:lunar orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_orbit)___ .

The three selected companies are: ___E:Blue Origin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin)___ (et al.) with their ___E:Orbital Reef U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Reef)___ station concept, ___E:Nanoracks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanoracks)___ (et al.) with their ___E:Starlab Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starlab_Space_Station)___ concept, and ___E:Northrop Grumman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman)___ with a station concept based on the HALO-module for the Gateway station.
NASA has conducted many uncrewed and robotic spaceflight programs throughout its history.
More than 1,000 uncrewed missions have been designed to explore the Earth and the Solar System.
NASA executes a mission development framework to plan, select, develop, and operate robotic missions.

This framework defines cost, schedule and technical risk parameters to enable competitive selection of missions involving mission candidates that have been developed by principal investigators and their teams from across NASA, the broader US Government research and development stakeholders, and industry.
The mission development construct is defined by four umbrella programs.
The Explorer program derives its origin from the earliest days of the US Space program.

In current form, the program consists of three classes of systems – ___E:Small Explorers (SMEX) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer_program#Small_Explorers_(SMEX))___ , ___E:Medium Explorers (MIDEX) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer_program#Medium-Class_Explorers_(MIDEX))___ , and ___E:University-Class Explorers (UNEX) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer_program)___ missions.
The NASA Explorer program office provides frequent flight opportunities for moderate cost innovative solutions from the heliophysics and astrophysics science areas.
The Small Explorer missions are required to limit cost to NASA to below $150M (2022 dollars).
Medium class explorer missions have typically involved NASA cost caps of $350M.
The Explorer program office is based at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center.
The NASA Discovery program develops and delivers robotic spacecraft solutions in the planetary science domain.
Discovery enables scientists and engineers to assemble a team to deliver a solution against a defined set of objectives and competitively bid that solution against other candidate programs.

Cost caps vary but recent mission selection processes were accomplished using a $500M cost cap for NASA. The Planetary Mission Program Office is based at the NASA Marshall Space Flight Center and manages both the Discovery and New Frontiers missions.
The office is part of the Science Mission Directorate.

NASA Administrator Bill Nelson announced on June 2, 2021, that the DAVINCI+ and VERITAS missions were selected to launch to Venus in the late 2020s, having beat out competing proposals for missions to Jupiter's volcanic moon Io and Neptune's large moon ___E:Triton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triton_(moon))___ that were also selected as Discovery program finalists in early 2020. Each mission has an estimated cost of $500 million, with launches expected between 2028 and 2030. Launch contracts will be awarded later in each mission's development.
The New Frontiers program focuses on specific ___E:Solar System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System)___ exploration goals identified as top priorities by the planetary science community.
Primary objectives include Solar System exploration employing medium class spacecraft missions to conduct high-science-return investigations.
New Frontiers builds on the development approach employed by the Discovery program but provides for higher cost caps and schedule durations than are available with Discovery.
Cost caps vary by opportunity; recent missions have been awarded based on a defined cap of $1 billion.
The higher cost cap and projected longer mission durations result in a lower frequency of new opportunities for the program – typically one every several years.
OSIRIS-REx and New Horizons are examples of New Frontiers missions.

NASA has determined that the next opportunity to propose for the fifth round of New Frontiers missions will occur no later than the fall of 2024. Missions in NASA's New Frontiers Program tackle specific Solar System exploration goals identified as top priorities by the planetary science community.
Exploring the Solar System with medium-class spacecraft missions that conduct high-science-return investigations is NASA's strategy to further understand the Solar System.
Large strategic missions (formerly called Flagship missions) are strategic missions that are typically developed and managed by large teams that may span several NASA centers.
The individual missions become the program as opposed to being part of a larger effort (see Discovery, New Frontiers, etc.).
The ___E:James Webb Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)___ is a strategic mission that was developed over a period of more than 20 years.
Strategic missions are developed on an ad-hoc basis as program objectives and priorities are established.
Missions like Voyager, had they been developed today, would have been strategic missions.

Three of the Great Observatories were strategic missions (the ___E:Chandra X-ray Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory)___ , the ___E:Compton Gamma Ray Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_Gamma_Ray_Observatory)___ , and the ___E:Hubble Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope)___ ).
Europa Clipper is the next large strategic mission in development by NASA.
NASA continues to play a material role in exploration of the Solar System as it has for decades.

Ongoing missions have current science objectives with respect to more than five extraterrestrial bodies within the Solar System – Moon ( ___E:Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter)___ ), Mars ( Perseverance rover), Jupiter ( Juno ), asteroid ___E:Bennu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/101955_Bennu)___ ( OSIRIS-REx ), and Kuiper Belt Objects ( New Horizons ).

The Juno extended mission will make multiple flybys of the Jovian moon Io in 2023 and 2024 after flybys of ___E:Ganymede U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon))___ in 2021 and ___E:Europa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon))___ in 2022. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 continue to provide science data back to Earth while continuing on their outward journeys into interstellar space.

On November 26, 2011, NASA's ___E:Mars Science Laboratory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Science_Laboratory)___ mission was successfully launched for Mars. The Curiosity rover successfully landed on Mars on August 6, 2012, and subsequently began its search for evidence of past or present life on Mars.

In September 2014, NASA's MAVEN spacecraft, which is part of the ___E:Mars Scout Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Scout_Program)___ , successfully entered Mars orbit and, as of October 2022, continues its study of the ___E:atmosphere of Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Mars)___ .
NASA's ongoing Mars investigations include in-depth surveys of Mars by the Perseverance rover.
NASA's Europa Clipper , launched in October 2024, will study the Galilean moon Europa through a series of flybys while in orbit around Jupiter.
Dragonfly will send a mobile robotic ___E:rotorcraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorcraft)___ to Saturn's biggest moon, ___E:Titan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(moon))___ .
As of May 2021, Dragonfly is scheduled for launch in June 2027.
The NASA Science Mission Directorate Astrophysics division manages the agency's astrophysics science portfolio.
NASA has invested significant resources in the development, delivery, and operations of various forms of space telescopes.
These telescopes have provided the means to study the cosmos over a large range of the electromagnetic spectrum.
The Great Observatories that were launched in the 1980s and 1990s have provided a wealth of observations for study by physicists across the planent.

The first of them, the ___E:Hubble Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope)___ , was delivered to orbit in 1990 and continues to function, in part due to prior servicing missions performed by the Space Shuttle.

The other remaining active great observatories include the ___E:Chandra X-ray Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory)___ (CXO), launched by ___E:STS-93 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-93)___ in July 1999 and is now in a 64-hour ___E:elliptical orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptical_orbit)___ studying X-ray sources that are not readily viewable from terrestrial observatories.

The ___E:Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaging_X-ray_Polarimetry_Explorer)___ (IXPE) is a space observatory designed to improve the understanding of X-ray production in objects such as neutron stars and pulsar wind nebulae, as well as stellar and supermassive black holes.
IXPE launched in December 2021 and is an international collaboration between NASA and the ___E:Italian Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Space_Agency)___ (ASI).
It is part of the NASA ___E:Small Explorers program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorers_Program)___ (SMEX) which designs low-cost spacecraft to study heliophysics and astrophysics.

The ___E:Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gehrels_Swift_Observatory)___ was launched in November 2004 and is a gamma-ray burst observatory that also monitors the afterglow in X-ray, and UV/Visible light at the location of a burst.

The mission was developed in a joint partnership between ___E:Goddard Space Flight Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Space_Flight_Center)___ (GSFC) and an international consortium from the United States, United Kingdom, and Italy. ___E:Pennsylvania State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University)___ operates the mission as part of NASA's ___E:Medium Explorer program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer_program)___ (MIDEX).

The ___E:Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_Gamma-ray_Space_Telescope)___ (FGST) is another gamma-ray focused space observatory that was launched to ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ in June 2008 and is being used to perform ___E:gamma-ray astronomy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma-ray_astronomy)___ observations.

In addition to NASA, the mission involves the ___E:United States Department of Energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy)___ , and government agencies in France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and Sweden.

The ___E:James Webb Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope)___ (JWST), launched in December 2021 on an ___E:Ariane 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariane_5)___ rocket, operates in a ___E:halo orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_orbit)___ circling the Sun-Earth ___E:L2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_point#L2)___ point.
JWST's high sensitivity in the infrared spectrum and its imaging resolution will allow it to view more distant, faint, or older objects than its predecessors, including Hubble.

NASA Earth Science is a large, umbrella program comprising a range of terrestrial and space-based collection systems in order to better understand the Earth system and its response to natural and human-caused changes.
Numerous systems have been developed and fielded over several decades to provide improved prediction for weather, climate, and other changes in the natural environment.

Several of the current operating spacecraft programs include: ___E:Aqua U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(satellite))___ ,  ___E:Aura U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aura_(satellite))___ ,  ___E:Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiting_Carbon_Observatory_2)___ (OCO-2),  ___E:Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-on (GRACE FO) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GRACE_and_GRACE-FO#GRACE_Follow-On)___ ,  and ___E:Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite 2 (ICESat-2) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICESat-2)___ .

In addition to systems already in orbit, NASA is designing a new set of Earth Observing Systems to study, assess, and generate responses for climate change, natural hazards, forest fires, and real-time agricultural processes.
The GOES-T satellite (designated ___E:GOES-18 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GOES-18)___ after launch) joined the fleet of US geostationary weather monitoring satellites in March 2022.
NASA also maintains the Earth Science Data Systems (ESDS) program to oversee the life cycle of NASA's Earth science data – from acquisition through processing and distribution.
The primary goal of ESDS is to maximize the scientific return from NASA's missions and experiments for research and applied scientists, decision makers, and society at large.
The Earth Science program is managed by the Earth Science Division of the NASA Science Mission Directorate.
NASA invests in various ground and space-based infrastructures to support its science and exploration mandate.
The agency maintains access to suborbital and orbital space launch capabilities and sustains ground station solutions to support its evolving fleet of spacecraft and remote systems.
The NASA Deep Space Network ( DSN ) serves as the primary ground station solution for NASA's interplanetary spacecraft and select Earth-orbiting missions.
The system employs ground station complexes near Barstow, California, in Spain near Madrid, and in Australia near Canberra.

The placement of these ground stations approximately 120 degrees apart around the planet provides the ability for communications to spacecraft throughout the ___E:Solar System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System)___ even as the Earth rotates about its axis on a daily basis.
The system is controlled at a 24x7 operations center at JPL in Pasadena, California, which manages recurring communications linkages with up to 40 spacecraft.
The system is managed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

The Near Space Network (NSN) provides telemetry, commanding, ground-based tracking, data and communications services to a wide range of customers with satellites in low earth orbit (LEO), geosynchronous orbit (GEO), highly elliptical orbits (HEO), and lunar orbits.

The NSN accumulates ground station and antenna assets from the Near-Earth Network and the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System ( TDRS ) which operates in geosynchronous orbit providing continuous real-time coverage for launch vehicles and low earth orbit NASA missions.

The NSN consists of 19 ground stations worldwide operated by the US Government and by contractors including Kongsberg Satellite Services (KSAT), Swedish Space Corporation (SSC), and South African National Space Agency (SANSA).

The ground network averages between 120 and 150 spacecraft contacts a day with TDRS engaging with systems on a near-continuous basis as needed; the system is managed and operated by the Goddard Space Flight Center.

The NASA Sounding Rocket Program ( NSRP ) is located at the ___E:Wallops Flight Facility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallops_Flight_Facility)___ and provides launch capability, payload development and integration, and field operations support to execute suborbital missions.

The program has been in operation since 1959 and is managed by the Goddard Space Flight Center using a combined US Government and contractor team.  The NSRP team conducts approximately 20 missions per year from both Wallops and other launch locations worldwide to allow scientists to collect data "where it occurs".
The program supports the strategic vision of the Science Mission Directorate collecting important scientific data for earth science, heliophysics, and astrophysics programs.

In June 2022, NASA conducted its first rocket launch from a commercial spaceport outside the US. It launched a ___E:Black Brant IX U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Brant_IX)___ from the ___E:Arnhem Space Centre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem_Space_Centre)___ in Australia.

The NASA Launch Services Program (LSP) is responsible for procurement of launch services for NASA uncrewed missions and oversight of launch integration and launch preparation activity, providing added quality and mission assurance to meet program objectives.

Since 1990, NASA has purchased ___E:expendable launch vehicle launch services U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expendable_launch_system)___ directly from commercial providers, whenever possible, for its scientific and applications missions.
Expendable launch vehicles can accommodate all types of orbit inclinations and altitudes and are ideal vehicles for launching Earth-orbit and interplanetary missions.
LSP operates from Kennedy Space Center and falls under the NASA Space Operations Mission Directorate (SOMD).

The Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate ( ARMD ) is one of five mission ___E:directorates U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/directorate)___ within NASA, the other four being the Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate, the Space Operations Mission Directorate, the ___E:Science Mission Directorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Mission_Directorate)___ , and the Space Technology Mission Directorate.

The ARMD is responsible for NASA's ___E:aeronautical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics)___ research, which benefits the ___E:commercial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_aviation)___ , ___E:military U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_aviation)___ , and ___E:general aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation)___ sectors.

ARMD performs its aeronautics research at four NASA facilities: ___E:Ames Research Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames_Research_Center)___ and ___E:Armstrong Flight Research Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong_Flight_Research_Center)___ in California, ___E:Glenn Research Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Research_Center)___ in Ohio, and ___E:Langley Research Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langley_Research_Center)___ in Virginia.
The NASA X-57 Maxwell is an experimental aircraft being developed by NASA to demonstrate the technologies required to deliver a highly efficient all-electric aircraft.
The primary goal of the program is to develop and deliver all-electric technology solutions that can also achieve airworthiness certification with regulators.
The program involves development of the system in several phases, or modifications, to incrementally grow the capability and operability of the system.
The initial configuration of the aircraft has now completed ground testing as it approaches its first flights.

In mid-2022, the X-57 was scheduled to fly before the end of the year.  The development team includes staff from the NASA Armstrong, Glenn, and Langley centers along with number of industry partners from the United States and Italy.

NASA is collaborating with the ___E:Federal Aviation Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration)___ and industry stakeholders to modernize the United States ___E:National Airspace System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Airspace_System)___ (NAS).

Efforts began in 2007 with a goal to deliver major modernization components by 2025.  The modernization effort intends to increase the safety, efficiency, capacity, access, flexibility, predictability, and resilience of the NAS while reducing the ___E:environmental impact of aviation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_aviation)___ .
The Aviation Systems Division of NASA Ames operates the joint NASA/FAA North Texas Research Station.
The station supports all phases of NextGen research, from concept development to prototype system field evaluation.

This facility has already transitioned advanced NextGen concepts and technologies to use through technology transfers to the FAA.  NASA contributions also include development of advanced automation concepts and tools that provide air traffic controllers, pilots, and other airspace users with more accurate real-time information about the nation's traffic flow, weather, and routing.

Ames' advanced airspace modeling and simulation tools have been used extensively to model the flow of air traffic flow across the US, and to evaluate new concepts in airspace design, traffic flow management, and optimization.

NASA has made use of technologies such as the ___E:multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-mission_radioisotope_thermoelectric_generator)___ (MMRTG), which is a type of ___E:radioisotope thermoelectric generator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioisotope_thermoelectric_generator)___ used to power spacecraft.
Shortages of the required ___E:plutonium-238 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-238)___ have curtailed deep space missions since the turn of the millennium.
An example of a spacecraft that was not developed because of a shortage of this material was New Horizons 2 .
In July 2021, NASA announced contract awards for development of ___E:nuclear thermal propulsion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_thermal_rocket)___ reactors.

Three contractors will develop individual designs over 12 months for later evaluation by NASA and the ___E:US Department of Energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy)___ .
NASA's space nuclear technologies portfolio are led and funded by its Space Technology Mission Directorate.

In January 2023, NASA announced a partnership with Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency ( ___E:DARPA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA)___ ) on the ___E:Demonstration Rocket for Agile Cislunar Operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonstration_Rocket_for_Agile_Cislunar_Operations)___ (DRACO) program to demonstrate a NTR engine in space, an enabling capability for NASA missions to Mars.  In July 2023, NASA and DARPA jointly announced the award of $499 million to Lockheed Martin to design and build an experimental NTR rocket to be launched in 2027.

In July 2025, Acting NASA Administrator Sean Duffy issued a directive to fast-track plans for placing a nuclear reactor on the Moon to support the agency's Artemis program and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.
The directive, prompted by concerns that China and Russia may deploy a joint lunar reactor by the mid-2030s, emphasizes the need for a 100-kilowatt system to power long-term lunar missions.
Duffy warned that if another nation establishes a reactor first, it could create "keep-out zones" limiting U.S. access.
Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC), founded in 1994, "focuses on archiving and distributing data related to human interactions in the environment.

SEDAC has extensive ___E:geospatial data U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geospatial_data)___ holdings.

In 2024, NASA was tasked by the ___E:US Government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States)___ to create a ___E:Time standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_standard)___ for the ___E:Moon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon)___ .

NASA's ___E:Human Research Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Research_Program)___ (HRP) is designed to study the effects of space on human health and also to provide countermeasures and technologies for human space exploration.

The medical effects of space exploration are reasonably limited in low Earth orbit or in travel to the Moon. Travel to Mars is significantly longer and deeper into space, significant medical issues can result.
These include bone density loss, radiation exposure, vision changes, circadian rhythm disturbances, heart remodeling, and immune alterations.

In order to study and diagnose these ill-effects, HRP has been tasked with identifying or developing small portable instrumentation with low mass, volume, and power to monitor the health of astronauts.

To achieve this aim, on May 13, 2022, NASA and ___E:SpaceX Crew-4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-4)___ astronauts successfully tested its rHEALTH ONE universal biomedical analyzer for its ability to identify and analyzer biomarkers, cells, microorganisms, and proteins in a spaceflight environment.

NASA established the Planetary Defense Coordination Office ( PDCO ) in 2016 to catalog and track potentially hazardous ___E:near-Earth objects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-Earth_object)___ (NEO), such as ___E:asteroids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid)___ and ___E:comets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet)___ and develop potential responses and defenses against these threats.

The PDCO is chartered to provide timely and accurate information to the government and the public on close approaches by ___E:Potentially hazardous objects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potentially_hazardous_objects)___ (PHOs) and any potential for impact.
The office functions within the Science Mission Directorate ___E:Planetary Science Division U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_Science_Division)___ .

The PDCO augmented prior cooperative actions between the United States, the European Union, and other nations which had been scanning the sky for NEOs since 1998 in an effort called ___E:Spaceguard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceguard)___ .
From the 1990s NASA has run many NEO detection programs from Earth bases observatories, greatly increasing the number of objects that have been detected.

Many asteroids are very dark and those near the Sun are much harder to detect from Earth-based telescopes which observe at night, and thus face away from the Sun. NEOs inside Earth orbit only reflect a part of light also rather than potentially a "full Moon" when they are behind the Earth and fully lit by the Sun.

In 1998, the ___E:United States Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ gave NASA a mandate to detect 90% of near-Earth asteroids over 1 km (0.62 mi) diameter (that threaten global devastation) by 2008.  This initial mandate was met by 2011.  In 2005, the original USA Spaceguard mandate was extended by the ___E:George E. Brown, Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Brown,_Jr.)___ Near-Earth Object Survey Act, which calls for NASA to detect 90% of NEOs with diameters of 140 m (460 ft) or greater, by 2020 (compare to the 20-meter ___E:Chelyabinsk meteor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelyabinsk_meteor)___ that hit Russia in 2013).
As of January 2020 [update] , it is estimated that less than half of these have been found, but objects of this size hit the Earth only about once in 2,000 years.

NASA has incorporated planetary defense objectives into several ongoing missions.

In 1999, NASA visited ___E:433 Eros U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/433_Eros)___ with the NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft which entered its orbit in 2000, closely imaging the asteroid with various instruments at that time.  NEAR Shoemaker became the first spacecraft to successfully orbit and land on an asteroid, improving our understanding of these bodies and demonstrating our capacity to study them in greater detail.

___E:OSIRIS-REx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSIRIS-REx)___ used its suite of instruments to transmit radio tracking signals and capture optical images of ___E:Bennu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/101955_Bennu)___ during its study of the asteroid that will help NASA scientists determine its precise position in the solar system and its exact orbital path. As Bennu has the potential for recurring approaches to the Earth-Moon system in the next 100–200 years, the precision gained from OSIRIS-REx will enable scientists to better predict the future gravitational interactions between Bennu and our planet and resultant changes in Bennu's onward flight path.
The ___E:WISE/NEOWISE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wide-field_Infrared_Survey_Explorer)___ mission was launched by NASA JPL in 2009 as an infrared-wavelength astronomical space telescope.

NASA and ___E:Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Applied_Physics_Laboratory)___ (JHAPL) jointly developed the first planetary defense purpose-built satellite, the ___E:Double Asteroid Redirection Test U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Asteroid_Redirection_Test)___ (DART) to test possible planetary defense concepts.

Scientists were seeking to determine whether an impact could alter the subsequent path of the asteroid; a concept that could be applied to future planetary defense.
On September 26, 2022, DART hit its target.

In the weeks following impact, NASA declared DART a success, confirming it had shortened Dimorphos' orbital period around Didymos by about 32 minutes, surpassing the pre-defined success threshold of 73 seconds.

___E:NEO Surveyor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEO_Surveyor)___ , formerly called the Near-Earth Object Camera (NEOCam) mission, is a space-based ___E:infrared telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_telescope)___ under development to survey the ___E:Solar System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System)___ for ___E:potentially hazardous asteroids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potentially_hazardous_object)___ .

In June 2022, the head of the NASA ___E:Science Mission Directorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Mission_Directorate)___ , ___E:Thomas Zurbuchen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Zurbuchen)___ , confirmed the start of ___E:NASA's UAP independent study team U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA%27s_UAP_independent_study_team)___ .

In response to the ___E:Apollo 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_1)___ accident, which killed three astronauts in 1967, Congress directed NASA to form an Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel (ASAP) to advise the NASA Administrator on safety issues and hazards in NASA's air and space programs.

NASA and NOAA have cooperated for decades on the development, delivery and operation of polar and geosynchronous weather satellites.

The relationship typically involves NASA developing the space systems, launch solutions, and ground control technology for the satellites and NOAA operating the systems and delivering weather forecasting products to users.

Multiple generations of NOAA Polar orbiting platforms have operated to provide detailed imaging of weather from low altitude.  ___E:Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostationary_Operational_Environmental_Satellites)___ (GOES) provide near-real-time coverage of the western hemisphere to ensure accurate and timely understanding of developing weather phenomenon.

The ___E:Landsat program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landsat_program)___ is the longest-running enterprise for acquisition of ___E:satellite imagery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_imagery)___ of Earth.
It is a joint NASA / ___E:USGS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey)___ program.
On July 23, 1972, the Earth Resources Technology Satellite was launched.
This was eventually renamed to Landsat 1 in 1975.  The most recent satellite in the series, Landsat 9 , was launched on September 27, 2021.
The instruments on the Landsat satellites have acquired millions of images.

The images, archived in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ and at Landsat receiving stations around the world, are a unique resource for global change research and applications in ___E:agriculture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture)___ , ___E:cartography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartography)___ , ___E:geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology)___ , ___E:forestry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry)___ , ___E:regional planning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_planning)___ , ___E:surveillance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance)___ and ___E:education U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education)___ , and can be viewed through the US Geological Survey (USGS) "EarthExplorer" website.

The collaboration between NASA and USGS involves NASA designing and delivering the space system (satellite) solution, launching the satellite into orbit with the USGS operating the system once in orbit.
As of October 2022, nine satellites have been built with eight of them successfully operating in orbit.
NASA collaborates with the European Space Agency on a wide range of scientific and exploration requirements.

From participation with the Space Shuttle (the Spacelab missions) to major roles on the Artemis program (the Orion Service Module), ESA and NASA have supported the science and exploration missions of each agency.

NASA and Roscosmos have cooperated on the development and operation of the International Space Station since September 1993.  The agencies have used launch systems from both countries to deliver station elements to orbit.

Both countries provide access to the station via launch systems noting Russia's unique role as the sole provider of delivery of crew and cargo upon retirement of the space shuttle in 2011 and prior to commencement of NASA COTS and crew flights.

Current geopolitical conditions in late 2022 make it unlikely that cooperation will be extended to other programs such as Artemis or lunar exploration.

The exhaust gases produced by rocket propulsion systems, both in Earth's atmosphere and in space, can adversely affect the Earth's environment.

Some ___E:hypergolic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergolic)___ rocket propellants, such as ___E:hydrazine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrazine)___ , are highly toxic prior to ___E:combustion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustion)___ , but decompose into less toxic compounds after burning.
Rockets using hydrocarbon fuels, such as ___E:kerosene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerosene)___ , release carbon dioxide and soot in their exhaust.

Carbon dioxide emissions are insignificant compared to those from other sources; on average, the United States consumed 803 million US gal (3.0 million m 3 ) of liquid fuels per day in 2014, while a single ___E:Falcon 9 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9)___ rocket first stage burns around 25,000 US gallons (95 m 3 ) of kerosene fuel per launch.

Even if a Falcon 9 were launched every single day, it would only represent 0.006% of liquid fuel consumption (and carbon dioxide emissions) for that day. Additionally, the exhaust from ___E:LOx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LOx)___ - and ___E:LH2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LH2)___ - fueled engines, like the ___E:SSME U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSME)___ , is almost entirely water vapor.

NASA addressed environmental concerns with its canceled ___E:Constellation program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program)___ in accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act in 2011.  In contrast, ___E:ion engines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_engines)___ use harmless noble gases like ___E:xenon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenon)___ for propulsion.
An example of NASA's environmental efforts is the ___E:NASA Sustainability Base U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Sustainability_Base)___ .

In 2018, NASA along with other companies including Sensor Coating Systems, ___E:Pratt & Whitney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_%26_Whitney)___ , Monitor Coating and ___E:UTRC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Technologies_Corp)___ launched the project CAUTION (CoAtings for Ultra High Temperature detectION).
